query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A data-driven machine learning model trained on both defect-inclusive simulation data and experimental measurements, including samples with ~1 wt.% oxygen, will predict the temperature‐dependent electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than conventional analytical models based on perfect crystals. Specifically, the model will capture enhanced impurity and defect scattering effects at 0–200 K and phonon-dominated scattering at 300–1200 K, yielding predictions within ±20% of experimental measurements for both regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy, considered both in its ideal defect‐free crystalline state and in a realistic state containing ~1 wt.% oxygen impurities.
generation.intervention: Training and application of a machine learning regression model using curated datasets from defect‐inclusive simulations and experimental conductivity measurements.
generation.conditions: Test over two temperature regimes: low (0–200 K) where quantum and impurity scattering effects dominate, and high (300–1200 K) where phonon scattering is predominant. The high-temperature regime measurements are performed on a sample containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.structural_mediator: Temperature-dependent scattering centers arising from defects and incorporated oxygen impurities that alter electron transport paths.
generation.mechanism: By learning complex correlations between defect structures, impurity concentrations, and temperature effects, the machine learning model accounts for scattering contributions that are neglected in conventional perfect-crystal analytical models. This leads to more realistic predictions for conductivity that span both cryogenic and elevated temperature regimes.
generation.predicted_outcome: The machine learning model will predict electrical conductivity values that agree with experimental measurements within a ±20% error margin across both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes, outperforming predictions from traditional analytical models limited to defect‐free crystals.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical approaches based solely on perfect, defect‐free crystal assumptions that do not include defect or oxygen impurity scattering effects.
generation.boundary: Applicability is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloys under controlled conditions where the defect structures are representative and with the notable inclusion of ~1 wt.% oxygen for high-temperature measurements; outside of these conditions (e.g., extreme impurity levels or different fabrication processes) the model’s accuracy may degrade.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative error margins and the sensitivity to variations in defect distributions are uncertain, and systematic deviations may arise if the curated datasets do not adequately capture real-world microstructural variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with well-characterized defect distributions and controlled addition of ~1 wt.% oxygen. Measure electrical conductivity across the two defined temperature regimes (0–200 K and 300–1200 K) using established methods. Compare the measured conductivity values with the predictions of both the machine learning model and existing analytical models.
measurements: Electrical conductivity (S/m) at several temperatures in the 0–200 K regime.
Electrical conductivity (S/m) at several temperatures in the 300–1200 K regime, particularly focusing on the room-temperature measurement for the oxygen-doped sample.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the machine learning model's predicted conductivity for the oxygen-containing sample deviates by more than 20% from the experimentally measured conductivity in any of the specified temperature regimes, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are designed for high elevated-temperature strength, with both edge and screw dislocations playing an important role for plastic deformation. However, they can also display a significant energetic driving force for chemical short-range ordering (SRO). Here, we investigate mechanisms underlying the mobilities of screw and edge dislocations in the body-centered cubic MoNbTaW RHEA over a wide temperature range using extensive molecular dynamics simulations based on a highly-accurate machine-learning interatomic potential. Further, we specifically evaluate how these mechanisms are affected by the presence of SRO. The mobility of edge dislocations is found to be enhanced by the presence of SRO, whereas the rate of double-kink nucleation in the motion of screw dislocations is reduced, although this influence of SRO appears to be attenuated at increasing temperature. Independent of the presence of SRO, a cross-slip locking mechanism is observed for the motion of screws, which provides for extra strengthening for refractory high-entropy alloy system.

frame.system: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy, considered both in its ideal (defect‐free) crystalline state and in a realistic state containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen impurities.
frame.goal: To develop a predictive method that accurately accounts for defect and impurity scattering—in addition to intrinsic temperature‐dependent effects—in order to predict transport properties (specifically conductivity) over wide temperature ranges.
frame.limitation: Existing analytical predictions suffer from limited accuracy because they are based on models for perfect, defect‐free crystals and thus do not capture the scattering induced by defects or oxygen impurities, especially across the low (0–200 K) and high (300–1200 K) temperature regimes.
root_cause_cues: limited accuracy of available analytical predictions
usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals
constraints: Temperature regimes: nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K
Specimen composition: must include tests on a sample with 1 wt.% oxygen
Must offer a held-out conductivity benchmark with a clearly defined falsification threshold
frame.regime: The model must operate in two distinct temperature regimes: (i) a low-temperature regime (0–200 K) where quantum and impurity scattering effects dominate, and (ii) a high-temperature regime (300–1200 K) where phonon scattering is predominant.
prior_attempts: Analytical approaches that assume perfect, defect-free crystal structures
Existing predictions that neglect the role of oxygen and defect-induced scattering, leading to quantitative inconsistencies with experimental measurements
frame.understanding: By incorporating temperature-dependent defect and impurity scattering mechanisms into the predictive framework, the new approach should yield improved quantitative conductivity predictions. Its advantage over existing methods is expected to arise from (i) a more realistic treatment of the microstructural effects (such as the scattering contributions from 1 wt.% oxygen impurities) and (ii) the ability to span two very different temperature regimes, thereby capturing both quantum-dominated and thermally activated transport phenomena. A specific falsification of the hypothesis would occur if, upon testing against a held-out conductivity benchmark (e.g., if the predicted room-temperature electrical conductivity for the oxygen-doped sample deviates by more than 20% from experimental data), the model fails to predict conductivity trends across both temperature regimes.
